analysis.one_liner: UltraTech Cement, part of the Aditya Birla Group, is India's largest cement maker, producing grey cement, white cement and ready-mix concrete across India and a few overseas markets.
analysis.whats_happening: UltraTech reported Q2 FY27 (Jul-Sep 2026) results on 19 October 2026, just three days ago: revenue rose 18.9% year-on-year to ₹23,295 crore and profit rose 21.3% YoY to ₹1,501 crore, but profit fell roughly 42% from the June quarter as monsoon seasonality and a jump in coal and imported petcoke costs squeezed margins. Cement prices, which had softened in July-August, recovered sharply in September-October (up 7-10% month-on-month), and the stock rose about 3% post-results on that pricing recovery, per a Jefferies note.
analysis.plain_terms: This is the country's biggest cement company, selling into a market that is growing steadily on housing and infrastructure demand. The tension right now is that volumes are growing strongly (nearly 14% year-on-year) but the profit per tonne isn't keeping pace, because fuel costs have risen faster than cement prices could initially follow. The stock also costs more, relative to profit, than its main listed peers - a premium that only makes sense if its superior capital efficiency continues. Whether the recent price recovery holds is the near-term question that will decide if margins bounce back.
analysis.quarters: Q1 FY27 (Apr-Jun 2026): revenue ₹24,465 crore (+16% YoY), PAT ₹2,604 crore (+17.2% YoY), domestic volumes 39.2 million tonnes (+13.1% YoY), EBITDA margin around 21%, management called it the best-ever Q1 on revenue, profit and volumes. Q2 FY27 (Jul-Sep 2026): revenue ₹23,295 crore (+18.9% YoY), PAT ₹1,501 crore (+21.3% YoY) but down about 42.5% from Q1, volumes 38.2 million tonnes (+12.9% YoY), EBITDA margin compressed to roughly 16% as power and fuel costs per bag rose from ₹45 to ₹51.5. Management flagged this as cost-driven, not an accounting distortion, though the India Cements and Kesoram acquisitions are now consolidated into both periods, which inflates YoY volume and revenue growth versus the pre-acquisition base - worth keeping in mind when reading the growth percentages.
analysis.performance_read: No stock splits or demergers apply here, so the raw price series needs no adjustment. The stock is down 14.3% from its February 2026 peak of ₹12,791 and sits roughly in the middle of its 52-week range (₹10,155-₹12,791). Over 1 year it's down 7.9%, but that still beats the Nifty's -12.4% and crushes peer Ambuja's -35.4%. Over 3 and 5 years it has meaningfully outperformed both the Nifty and Ambuja. Over the last 3 months it has lagged the Nifty slightly (-6.1% vs -5.0%) while still beating Ambuja by a wide margin.
analysis.valuation_read: UltraTech trades at roughly 36x trailing earnings and about 4.3-4.4x book value, a clear premium to Ambuja Cement (around 25x P/E, 1.8x P/B) though cheaper than Shree Cement (around 59x P/E). Why it's expensive: its ROCE of roughly 13% and ROE of roughly 11% are well above Ambuja's (ROCE ~6%, ROE ~8%), reflecting scale, lower leverage, and more efficient capital use - the market is paying for quality and consistency, not hope. Whether that premium is justified depends on whether margins recover from the Q2 dip; a sustained margin shortfall would make the current multiple look expensive relative to peers.
analysis.growth_read: Growth here is clearly volume-led, not margin-led: domestic volumes grew 12.9-13.8% YoY in the last two quarters, ahead of the roughly 10% industry growth rate management cited, while EBITDA margin actually fell from ~21% to ~16% between Q1 and Q2 FY27 on rising fuel costs. In a commodity business like cement, this is a less durable growth pattern than margin expansion would be, since it depends on cement prices eventually catching up to cost inflation - which management says began happening in September-October 2026.
analysis.health_read: Leverage is low and improving (debt-to-equity around 0.27-0.30x, net debt around ₹17,900 crore against a company generating thousands of crores in quarterly profit), so financial risk looks modest. The real risk here is business/operating risk - cyclical cement pricing and volatile input costs (coal, imported petcoke) that can swing quarterly margins by 5 percentage points, as just happened. Whether operating cash flow is converting cleanly into profit this year is not verified - check the latest cash flow statement on Screener before relying on that specific ratio.
analysis.ownership_read: Promoters (Grasim Industries/the Aditya Birla Group) hold about 58.5% of the company, down slightly (0.85 percentage points) quarter-on-quarter, with zero shares pledged across all recent disclosed quarters - a clean picture on that front. A promoter-group entity, Pilani Investment and Industries Corporation, sold about 1.7 million shares via a block deal in August 2026, a modest trim rather than a change in control intent. Foreign institutional holding has been declining steadily, from about 18% in December 2023 to around 12% by September 2026, while domestic institutional holding has risen from about 14% to nearly 21% over the same period - a notable rotation from foreign to domestic ownership. No specific well-known individual investor was identified on the public shareholder register based on available data - not verified, check Screener for the latest named-shareholder list.
strengths: Domestic cement volumes grew 13.8% YoY in Q2 FY27, ahead of management's cited industry growth rate of about 10%
ROCE of roughly 13% is well above Ambuja Cement's ~6% and Shree Cement's ~11%, pointing to superior capital efficiency
Debt-to-equity of around 0.27-0.30x despite funding large acquisitions (Kesoram, India Cements) in recent years
Zero promoter share pledging across all recently disclosed quarters
watchpoints: EBITDA margin fell from roughly 21% in Q1 FY27 to roughly 16% in Q2 FY27 as coal and imported petcoke costs rose faster than cement prices
Foreign institutional ownership has declined from about 18% (Dec 2023) to about 12% (Sep 2026), even as domestic institutions have been buying - a rotation worth monitoring
Trades at roughly a 45% P/E premium to Ambuja Cement; that premium depends on margins recovering, since a prolonged shortfall could pressure the multiple
New diversification moves - a ₹1,800 crore entry into wires and cables (Ultravolt) and a renewable-energy stake - take management attention and capital outside the core cement business
analysis.one_thing: Whether the cement price recovery seen in September-October 2026 (up 7-10% month-on-month per management) holds through the Q3 FY27 (Oct-Dec) results, which would confirm pricing is catching up with fuel cost inflation and restoring margins toward the ~21% seen in Q1 FY27 rather than the ~16% seen in Q2.
analysis.data_notes: Quarterly results (Q1 and Q2 FY27 revenue, PAT, volumes, EBITDA) were cross-checked across the company's own press release, NSE filing coverage and multiple independent news outlets, which were consistent to within minor rounding. Valuation multiples (P/E, market cap) showed a wider spread across aggregators (P/E cited as both ~36x and ~42x, market cap ₹3.1-3.6 lakh crore) likely due to differing as-of dates and standalone vs consolidated bases - the more recent, better-corroborated cluster (P/E ~36x) was used. Could not verify exact operating-cash-flow-to-profit conversion or confirm/deny any specific named large individual investor on the shareholder register - check Screener directly for both.
